Constraint on that: a dent can be rubbed out by a crumb, but it can also be read by touch, and the sheet has been creased in thirds. The three words fall one to each panel. If it is folded along the old creases and pushed through a thumb-high slot, they reach a reader in reverse order, last word first. Whatever she wrote must therefore still make sense when it arrives backwards, or she wrote it knowing it would not.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
The three words are "Not yet. Come." Reversed, they arrive as "Come. Yet not," and the sentence survives the flip because the middle word hinges both ways. The full stop sits in the groove between panels, so the crease swallows it, and a reader at the slot cannot tell whether "Come" is an invitation or an order to stop.

Constraint on that: the middle panel's dent is the deepest of the three, deep enough to have cut through the paper into a pinhole, and only light from the east passes through it. The one reader who gets all three words in the right order is whoever stands on the quay at dawn, where the lens throws its point, and holds the folded sheet between the sun and the baker's window.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
The baker's window has its own constraint. The pane facing the sheet is frosted on the lower half, which blocks the pinhole's light unless the sheet is held high, at the height of someone standing on tiptoe or lifted. Only a small person, or a grown one who remembers being small, will find the angle where "Not yet. Come." clears the frost and falls whole on the flour-dusted sill.

The sill has a fact of its own: a ring in the flour, clean at the centre, ridged at the rim, where a bottle once stood and was moved. The last ring in the series was set there at dawn, and the light is now passing through its empty middle.

Your turn: one new fact, one constraint on it.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
The light passing through the ring's empty middle lands on a loaf cooling beside it, and the loaf's crust has been scored with a baker's blade in a pattern of three long cuts and one short, the usual decoration for that bakery's bread. The baker has scored every loaf that way for eleven years without knowing it meant anything.

Constraint on that: the short cut is the only one that does not run through to the crumb. It stops at the crust, a shallow nick, so it will not open in the oven. That makes it the one stroke on the loaf that cannot be eaten away, and whoever breaks the bread at the sill will find the fifth stroke already waiting, unscored, in the soft middle where no blade has been.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
The fifth stroke is waiting in the crumb, but not as a cut. It is a thread of dark: a single long hair-fine line of blue-black running through the soft middle, where ink was folded into the dough as it was kneaded. The baker has never seen it, because he always breaks loaves from the end and sells the halves unopened. Only a loaf broken across the scored face, at the sill, with the light behind it, would show the line.

Constraint on that: the thread runs the wrong way. A stroke kneaded in by a hand moving through dough would be curved and folded back on itself, but this one is dead straight, and it ends at a clean edge, as if the dough had been cut and rejoined around it. Someone laid a length of inked cord into the loaf before the last proof, a cord long enough to be pulled out whole by whoever has the nerve to tear the bread open and find the end.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
The cord is not string. It is a strip of the clerk's ruled paper, rolled tight and inked on one edge only, and when it is drawn out whole and unrolled it is exactly one ledger column long. Its single inked line is the thread, and the other face holds a row of eleven small round holes, pricked from the back, with a twelfth hole at the end that has been left unpierced, only dented.

Constraint on that: the baker's oven was lit before dawn by someone else, and a paper strip proofed inside a loaf would scorch at the crust but not in the middle. The strip is pale and clean, yet the dough around it has a faint brown halo, as if it had been baked with the ink already drying inside. So the strip went into the loaf after the dough was shaped and before the oven door closed, which leaves a window of a few minutes in which only the person who lit the oven could have set it there.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
The person who lit the oven left a mark in the one place a baker would not look: the oven door's iron latch, which has a bright thumb-width scrape on its underside, where a hand reached up from below to lift it. The baker is tall, and the latch is set at his shoulder, so he lifts it from above and the underside is worn dull. This scrape is fresh and low, made by someone who had to reach up, so the one who lit the oven was smaller than the baker, and small enough to need the stool.

Constraint on that: the stool is where the story's count goes wrong. It stands against the oven with three legs polished by use and a fourth, shorter leg shimmed with a folded wad of paper. The wad is a ruled slip, pricked from the back, and it carries the twelfth hole's missing partner: a dented spot that would match the strip's unpierced end exactly if the two were laid together. Whoever stood on the stool to set the strip in the loaf had to take it out again to sit steady, so the baker's stool kept the half of the message that the loaf could not hold.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
The slip under the short leg has been flattened by years of weight, and when it is laid beside the strip, the two dents do not just match. They share a crease, and the crease runs through the middle of a faint word pressed into the slip's underside by the stool's own foot: "Marguerite." The shimmed leg has been spelling the name against the floor every time the baker sat down, correctly, with all its letters.

Constraint on that: the final E is the only letter the foot has not pressed. The leg's edge is rounded there, worn away by a sideways scuff, so the name on the slip is complete only when the stool is tilted, one leg lifted, the way a child tips a chair back to reach something on a high shelf. Anyone who sits squarely on it reads the name one stroke short, and anyone who tips it finishes the word.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
The tipped stool has its own witness: the floor under the short leg. When the stool tilts, the lifted leg's shadow falls across a pale boards-width of flour, and in that strip someone has drawn a single vertical with a smaller stroke after it, the shape of the unpressed E, in a finger's trail. The child, or someone who remembers being one, tipped the stool, read the name one stroke short, and finished it in flour where the baker sweeps every night.

Constraint on that: the baker sweeps at closing, so the stroke should be gone each morning, yet it is crisp and unscuffed. A stroke that survives a nightly sweep was redrawn every dawn by the same hand, and the broom's bristles have a bare patch worn exactly one finger-width wide, as if the baker had learned, without ever noticing, to lift his broom over that one place.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
The broom's bare patch has a second source. A broom lifted by habit leaves its wear on the shaft side, where the grip shifts, but here the wear is on the bristle tips alone, worn flat as if pressed down on something soft and returned to the same spot each night. The baker was not stepping over the stroke. He was setting the broom down on it, gently, the way you lay a hand on a sleeping shoulder, and leaving it there while he thought about something else.

Constraint on that: the flour under the bare patch is not his flour. It is a coarse, greyish meal ground from the lighthouse's supply tin of ship's biscuit, which no harbour baker stocks, so each dawn's stroke was drawn in a medium carried from the north, a pinch at a time, and the pinch has been getting smaller. Tonight's stroke is the first one drawn with white harbour flour, and the grey is gone from the boards for good.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
The white stroke is drawn, and it is the first in the series with no bottom edge. The grey strokes were laid with a finger pressed hard, so each had a ridge at its base where the meal piled up. This one was made by a flat palm drawn lightly sideways, so the line is wide, soft and blurred at both edges. It is a gesture of wiping, not of writing, and the flour looks less like a letter than like a place where a letter used to be and has been politely cleared.

Constraint on that: the palm that cleared it left its own print at the stroke's near end, and it is the size of an adult's. Under the bare patch in the boards, the grey meal is not gone but swept into the knothole beside it, packed flush. The baker did not lose the old medium by accident. He gathered each night's grey, one pinch at a time, and kept it. The knothole now holds eleven years of it, a small grey tally in the floor.

Your turn: one new fact, one constraint on it.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
The knothole's grey is not loose. It is layered, and a sliver of it lifted on a pin shows the layers as bands, each one slightly paler than the one beneath, because the biscuit meal was cut with a little more harbour flour every year. Eleven bands, darkest at the bottom, so the hole is a core sample of the baker's slow shift from the lighthouse's medium to his own, and the top band is nearly white.

Constraint on that: the bands are not evenly spaced. The seventh is twice as thick as its neighbours, and the pale seam inside it is where a whole year's pinches were poured in at once. That was the year the baker was ill, or away, and someone else kept his count for him, so the grey tally has one stretch that was not his hand, and the broom, bare-patched and set down gently, was always being held by two people in turn.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
The second hand in the seventh band left a trace that the baker could never have made: a single hair, caught in the layer and baked in by the flour's own damp. It is not grey or white but blue-black, and it is straight, a bristle rather than a hair, cut from a pen's old quill-brush or a very fine paintbrush. Someone who tends ink kept the count that year, and the knothole's one thick band is a year of the waiter's own hand, brought south and set into the floor.

Constraint on that: the bristle has been bent once, sharply, at its midpoint, and the bend is a hinge, not a break. It was folded around a pin when the layer was lifted, which means somebody else lifted this sliver before today, put the bristle back exactly as it lay, and left no other mark. The core sample has already been read once, by a hand careful enough to restore what it found, and careful enough that we only know because of one fold.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
The fold has a second crease that matches no pin. Under a lens, the bristle bends again a hair's width from the first, in the opposite direction, so it was not just lifted on a pin and laid back. It was pinched between two fingertips and straightened, the way you flatten a thread before knotting it. The first hand who read the core also repaired it, with the patience of someone who has spent years smoothing pricked paper.

Constraint on that: the restored bristle points to the knothole's rim, not along the layer as it was baked in. It was set pointing toward the door, toward the quay, toward whoever would next lift the sliver and follow it. The one careful reader did not just hide that they had been there. They left a direction, so that anyone sharp enough to notice the fold would also be told which way to look next.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
The bristle's direction has a flaw in its length. A pointer set toward the quay should end at something, but this one is too short to reach the door, and the floorboards between the knothole and the threshold hold no further marker, no flour, no grit, no dent. The direction is real, but it was set by someone who trusted the next reader to walk the rest by guessing, which means they did not expect a stranger. They expected someone who already knew the way, and the bristle is a courtesy, like a hand held out to a person who would have found the door anyway.

Constraint on that: the door's inside face has a single hook at the height of a small person's shoulder, and the hook is worn bright on its upper curve only. Nothing has hung there for years that weighed anything, but something light was hung and lifted every morning: a thin cord, one ledger column long, that was threaded through the hook to hold a folded sheet at the door as the baker opened up.

Your turn: one new fact, one constraint on it.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
The folded sheet held at the hook was never the copybook page. It was a blank, ruled in the clerk's columns and creased in thirds, hung so that anyone entering would brush it with a shoulder and set it swinging. Its only mark is a faint rectangle of cleaner paper on one panel, where something the size of a thumbnail was stuck down for years and peeled away: a label, a stamp, a seal.

Constraint on that: the cleaner rectangle has a rim of dried wax around three of its sides and none on the fourth, so whatever sat there was pressed on by thumb and lifted from the bottom edge, the same free edge as the registry's pasted slip. The thing it held could be read only by someone who lifted it, and the hook was set at the height of the one hand small enough to reach under the sheet without rattling it.
